**HYPOTHESIS (answer to the question):**

Effect size estimates tend to be larger in the original studies than in their replications in **all three disciplines — Social psychology, Cognitive psychology, and Experimental Economics — but the tendency is strongest in Social psychology**. Across the 86 original–replication pairs, the original effect exceeds the replication effect in ~85% of studies overall. By domain, the per-study "original > replication" share is Social 88% (30/34), Economics 83% (15/18), Cognitive 82% (28/34) — so by that count Social psychology shows the most pervasive attenuation, and it is also clearly the domain with the *largest magnitude* of shrinkage: its mean relative effect size (replication/original) is only 0.28 (median 0.13), versus 0.51 (median 0.65) in Cognitive psychology and 0.66 (median 0.70) in Experimental Economics. Social psychology additionally has the most sign reversals (10/34 replications flipped direction vs. 5/34 Cognitive and 3/18 Economics) and by far the lowest replication rate (21% vs. 47% and 61%). A formal test of the magnitude of attenuation across domains (Kruskal–Wallis on relative_es, H=8.34, p=0.016; Social vs. rest Mann–Whitney p=0.002) confirms Social psychology as the domain where original effect estimates most overstate replication effects, while the raw Fisher-z difference magnitudes are statistically similar across domains (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.54). In short: **every domain's original studies tend to overstate effects, with Social psychology the most affected domain and Experimental Economics the least.**

---

**SUPPORTING EVIDENCE**

Primary analysis — per-study paired differences on the Fisher-z scale (fiso − fisr):

| domain | n | orig > repl n (%) | mean dz | median dz | paired t p | Wilcoxon p | sign flips | attenuated (0<rel<1) | rel>1 | mean rel_es | median rel_es | replicated % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Social | 34 | 30 (88.2%) | 0.233 | 0.232 | 4e-07 | 1e-06 | 10 | 19 | 4 | 0.278 | 0.131 | 20.6% |
| Cognitive | 34 | 28 (82.4%) | 0.289 | 0.249 | 4.5e-05 | 6e-06 | 5 | 23 | 6 | 0.509 | 0.650 | 47.1% |
| Economics | 18 | 15 (83.3%) | 0.266 | 0.143 | 0.0067 | 0.0008 | 3 | 12 | 3 | 0.657 | 0.698 | 61.1% |
| **Overall** | **86** | **73 (84.9%)** | **0.262** | — | **7e-12** | **1.4e-11** | **18** | **54** | **13** | **0.449** | **0.427** | **39.5%** |

- Secondary lens (project): Psychology/rpp n=68 — 85.3% orig>repl, mean dz 0.261, 15 flips; Experimental Economics/ee n=18 — 83.3%, mean dz 0.266, 3 flips.
- Robustness: on the raw correlation scale (ro − rr) the per-domain proportions are identical (82.4/83.3/88.2%) and the sign of the difference agrees with the Fisher-z sign in 86/86 studies — scale choice does not affect conclusions.
- Sign-flip composition: of the 73 studies where the original is larger, 18 are qualitative sign reversals (rr < 0) and 55 are pure attenuation; all 18 flips are also non-replications (replicated = 0), a coherent pattern rather than data errors. Flip rates do not differ significantly across disciplines (chi-square p = 0.29).

Supplementary (labeled) — inverse-variance weighted pooled Fisher-z difference per domain (weights = 1/(se_fiso² + se_fisr²)):

| domain | pooled dz | SE | z | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Social | 0.208 | 0.024 | 8.62 | <0.001 |
| Cognitive | 0.206 | 0.038 | 5.48 | <0.001 |
| Economics | 0.013 | 0.033 | 0.40 | 0.69 |

The pooled view sharpens the contrast: Social and Cognitive psychology show statistically robust pooled attenuation of original vs. replication effects, whereas in Experimental Economics the weighted pooled difference is essentially zero — consistent with the ee project powering replications off the original effect size (mean relative_es 0.66, 61% replication rate), so per-study attenuation exists (83% of pairs) but does not survive precision-weighting.

**Workflow executed:** loaded the joined dataset (86 rows, no missing key fields); computed paired differences on Fisher-z and raw-r scales; per-discipline and per-project summaries of the proportion original > replication, mean/median differences with paired t and Wilcoxon tests; relative_es distribution statistics; sign-flip and attenuation counts; chi-square test of flip rates across disciplines; Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney tests of attenuation magnitude across domains; supplementary inverse-variance pooled comparison. Results saved to analysis/results_by_discipline.csv and analysis/results_by_project.csv.

**Assumptions & limitations:**
1. Domain = `discipline` column; this is confounded with replication project (Economics = ee only; Cognitive/Social = rpp only), so domain and project effects cannot be separated.
2. Per-study comparison of recorded estimates (not a full meta-regression); the pooled weighted comparison is supplementary and sensitive to within-domain heterogeneity.
3. Negative rr / relative_es treated as genuine sign reversals (they count toward "original larger"); relative_es is a signed ratio.
4. Mean dz magnitudes are similar across disciplines (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.54); the strongest cross-domain claim rests on relative_es (attenuation magnitude) and flip/replication rates, which favor Social psychology as the most affected domain.
5. Economics has the smallest n (18), so its per-domain estimates are less precise; its pooled result (dz ≈ 0) is notable but based on a single, well-powered replication project.

payload.hypothesis: Original studies show larger effect estimates than replications in all three disciplines, but the tendency is strongest in Social psychology (88% of pairs orig>repl; mean relative_es 0.28; 10/34 sign flips; 21% replication rate), intermediate in Cognitive psychology (82%; relative_es 0.51) and least pronounced in Experimental Economics (83%; relative_es 0.66; pooled weighted difference near zero).
